(CNN) -- Canadian ski resort gondola cars that were left dangling and swaying with terrified skiers inside failed because ice buildup snapped a supporting tower, the resort said Thursday. One gondola car is suspended above an icy creek at a ski resort near Whistler, British Columbia. In a rare occurrence called ice-jacking, water seeped into the lower section of the lift tower and turned to ice Tuesday at Whistler Blackcomb resort, 177 kilometers (110 miles) north of Vancouver, a resort official said in a press release Thursday. The lift hangs from a tower that is spliced into two parts. Extremely cold temperatures caused the ice buildup that exerted 800 tons of pressure between the two parts that hold the tower together, causing them to rupture, according to Whistler Blackcomb. The section of the lift affected by the accident had 15 cars going up the mountain and 15 coming down at the time, but they weren't carrying a lot of passengers, according to Doug Forseth, senior vice president of the resort. He said 53 passengers had been rescued from the stranded cars. No skiers at the Whistler, British Columbia, resort were seriously injured. "The towers are not normally designed to allow for any water penetration and so this failure is a very unusual situation," said Warren Sparks, senior vice president of Doppelmayr Canada, the engineering firm that investigated the accident. They are trying to figure out what caused the water to pool. He said independent structural engineers are examining the tower from Vancouver-based CVMM Consulting Engineers. "The evidence so far indicates a sudden rupture rather than a fatigue failure over an extended period," Sparks said. At least two gondola cars broke away and hit the ground, both from relatively low heights near the tower that split, and caused the system's heavy cable line to slacken, according to Tyler Noble, a reporter for CNNRadio affiliate CKNW in Vancouver. "One hit a bus stop and the other hit a house," Noble said Wednesday. "Another one was suspended over a creek, but everyone is out of that car." The broken Excaliber Gondola was not operating Thursday. Whistler engineers checked eight similar towers across the two mountains of the resort. All passed those inspections, and are open Thursday, the release said. The British Columbia Authority says it does not expect to rescind operating permits on any lifts at the resort, other than the Excaliber Gondola. Jeff Colburn, general manager of Silver Mountain Resort in Kellogg, Idaho, said a lift tower at his resort was similarly damaged by ice in December 2006. The damage was discovered in the morning before the slopes opened, so no one was endangered, he said. The damaged tower was replaced in about three weeks, Colburn said, and the resort's business was not significantly disrupted. "We check our towers in the summer now, and we also check before we open up for ski season as well just to make sure they don't have any water in them, and we've worked with the manufacturers," he said. Holes have been drilled in the bases of towers so that water can drain out, Colburn said. CNN's Ashley Fantz and Jim Kavanagh contributed to this report.

# The Science Behind the Snap: How "Ice-Jacking" Brought Down a Whistler Gondola Tower

On a clear, freezing day at Canada’s world-renowned Whistler Blackcomb resort, terror struck high above the snow-covered slopes. Without warning, a critical support tower for the resort’s busy gondola system suffered a catastrophic structural collapse. The sudden failure left 53 skiers and snowboarders suspended high in the air, trapped in dangling cabins, and sparked an immediate, high-stakes emergency response. 

Miraculously, thanks to swift rescue operations and the safety systems built into the gondola cabins, all stranded passengers were brought safely to the ground with no serious injuries reported. However, the incident left resort operators, ski lift manufacturers, and safety inspectors asking a critical question: how could a massive, heavy-duty steel tower engineered to withstand extreme alpine environments suddenly snap?

To answer this, a team of specialized structural engineers and forensic investigators was brought in to conduct an exhaustive autopsy of the ruptured lift structure. What they discovered was an extraordinary, silent mechanical failure—a rare phenomenon known to engineers as "ice-jacking."

### The Mechanics of "Ice-Jacking"

While steel towers are built to endure immense external forces—including high winds, heavy cable loads, and sub-zero temperatures—the investigation revealed that the enemy came from within. 

The process began long before the day of the collapse. Water from rain and melting snow had managed to seep into tiny, unseen cavities inside the hollow structure of the steel tower, likely entering through microscopic cracks or degraded seals. Because structural steel towers are typically sealed or equipped with drainage mechanisms to keep their interiors dry, the trapped water was unable to escape.

As the weather plunged back into freezing temperatures, the trapped water began to freeze. It is a fundamental law of physics that water expands by roughly 9% when it turns to ice. In an open environment, this expansion is harmless. However, contained within the rigid, unyielding interior of a heavy steel tower, the expanding ice acted like a slow-motion hydraulic ram. 

As temperatures cycled between melting and freezing, more water entered the cavity and froze, layer by layer. This cumulative process—ice-jacking—built up an astronomical amount of internal stress. 

### 800 Tons of Pressure

The engineering team’s structural analysis revealed staggering numbers. The expanding ice had generated an incredible **800 tons of internal outward pressure** against the walls of the steel structure. 

To put that into perspective, 800 tons is roughly equivalent to the weight of two fully loaded commercial airliners pressing outward against a localized section of steel. The intense pressure far exceeded the ultimate tensile strength of the tower's metal frame. The steel did not simply deform or bend gradually over time; instead, the extreme, localized stress reached a critical breaking point. Under the massive weight of the operational gondola line and the unseen internal pressure, the structural integrity failed, and the tower snapped suddenly and violently.

### Industry Impact and Legacy

The findings sent shockwaves through the alpine transit and structural engineering industries. While ice-jacking was a known theoretical risk in certain types of masonry and civil engineering, its occurrence as a primary cause of catastrophic failure in a modern steel lift tower was exceptionally rare. 

The Whistler Blackcomb incident served as a dramatic wake-up call for resort operators worldwide. In the aftermath of the investigation, ski resorts and engineering firms globally updated their maintenance and inspection protocols. Standard visual inspections were no longer considered sufficient. Today, lift infrastructure inspections regularly utilize non-destructive testing, ultrasonic measuring, thermal imaging, and enhanced internal drainage checks to ensure that water cannot collect inside sealed metal components.

Though the failure was a terrifying ordeal for the 53 skiers trapped above the snow, the thorough investigation that followed transformed a near-tragedy into a vital lesson in forensic engineering—ensuring that the silent threat of ice-jacking is kept at bay on mountain peaks across the world.

**Ice buildup causes Whistler Blackcomb gondola tower to fail, leaving passengers dangling in freezing cold**

**By** Eric Bradner, CNN
**Updated** 6:42 PM EST, Tue December 16, 2023

**(CNN) —** Dozens of skiers and snowboarders were rescued in sub-zero temperatures Tuesday after a massive buildup of ice caused a structural failure on a gondola tower at the Whistler Blackcomb ski resort, sending cabins plummeting toward the snow and leaving riders trapped high above the ground.

At least twelve people were treated for injuries, including fractures and hypothermia, after Tower 4 of the resort’s popular Excalibur Gondola sheared apart, according to local emergency responders. 

Resort officials confirmed that a rare meteorological phenomenon known as "ice jacking"—where water seeps into a hollow tower, freezes, expands, and exerts thousands of pounds of pressure—split the steel structure from the inside out.

The failure occurred shortly after 2:30 p.m. local time, causing the haul rope to drop suddenly. Two cabins slammed into the ground below, while a third caught on the roof of a nearby barn. Dozens of other cabins were left stranded along the upper stretch of the line in bitter, wind-whipped cold.

### 'We just heard a sound like thunder'

Eyewitnesses described a scene of sudden panic on what had otherwise been a standard afternoon on the slopes.

"We just heard a massive crack, like a lightning strike or thunder, and then the whole line dropped about 30 feet," said Sarah Jenkins, a tourist from Seattle who was trapped in a cabin three towers up from the collapse. "The cabin started swinging violently. We held onto each other for dear life. You could hear people screaming all the way down the mountain."

Jenkins and three others remained suspended nearly 50 feet in the air for more than two hours as temperatures dropped to -10°C (14°F).

Resort ski patrollers and local emergency crews acted swiftly, using complex high-angle rope rescue systems to lower terrified passengers one by one from the dangling cars. 

"Our team trained for worst-case scenarios, but this was a extremely complex technical rescue due to the steep terrain and dropping temperatures," said Whistler Fire Rescue Chief David Allen during a Tuesday evening press conference. "Our top priority was getting those people out before hypothermia set in."

All 53 trapped passengers were safely evacuated by 5:30 p.m., officials said.

### The science behind 'Ice Jacking'

Engineers and investigators are focusing on a recent cycle of extreme weather as the primary cause of the tower failure. Over the weekend, the Pacific Northwest resort experienced unusually heavy rainfall followed by an abrupt, deep freeze.

Resort officials believe water collected inside the upper section of the steel tower. When the temperature plunged overnight, the trapped water froze. Because ice expands by roughly 9% in volume, the immense pressure sheared the massive steel bolts holding the upper tower section together.

"This is an extraordinary and rare event," said Whistler Blackcomb General Manager Regional Director Mark Sills. "The safety of our guests is our absolute highest priority. We perform daily inspections on all our lifts, but the ice buildup occurred deep within the internal column of the tower, which was invisible from the outside."

Sills added that the gondola line will remain closed indefinitely while independent engineering teams and regulatory authorities conduct a thorough investigation into the structural integrity of the entire system.

### A shock to North America’s premier resort

Whistler Blackcomb, located in the Coast Mountains of British Columbia about 75 miles north of Vancouver, is the largest ski resort in North America, drawing more than two million visitors annually. 

Incidents involving major lift failures are exceptionally rare in North America, where strict safety regulations govern ski infrastructure. However, Tuesday's failure has raised immediate questions about how extreme weather patterns brought on by climate volatility might affect aging infrastructure at high altitudes.

British Columbia’s Safety Authority (Technical Safety BC) confirmed it has dispatched a team of senior investigators to the site.

For those stuck on the mountain Tuesday, the experience is one they won't soon forget.

"You never think the lift you’re riding is going to snap," said Jenkins, speaking from the base lodge wrapped in a thermal blanket. "I’m just glad to have my feet back on solid ground."

The incident, which saw a key support tower snap and drop two cabins to the ground, triggered a massive emergency response that successfully rescued 53 stranded passengers suspended high above the snow-covered slopes.

One cabin slammed onto the roof of a bus shelter below, while another plummeted into a nearby creek bed. Twelve people sustained minor injuries, but authorities confirmed that no fatalities occurred—a outcome officials called a "miracle" given the severity of the drop.

Speaking on behalf of the resort during the immediate aftermath, Doug Forseth, then-Senior Vice President of Operations for Whistler Blackcomb, emphasized the rapid response of emergency personnel and the shock of the structural failure.

"Our immediate priority was the safety and evacuation of our guests, and our mountain rescue teams performed impeccably under extremely challenging conditions," Forseth stated. "This was an unprecedented event for Whistler Blackcomb. A tower failure of this nature is something no one in the ski industry ever expects to see."

### Understanding "Ice-Jacking"

Following a thorough investigation by British Columbia’s Safety Authority (now Technical Safety BC) alongside independent engineers, the root cause was identified as "ice-jacking."

Ice-jacking occurs when water infiltrates a sealed or hollow metallic structure—in this case, the interior joint where two sections of the steel tower were spliced together. As ambient temperatures fluctuate, trapped water repeatedly freezes and expands. Because ice expands by roughly nine percent when it freezes, it generates thousands of pounds of hydraulic pressure per square inch. Over time, this relentless mechanical force slowly prying the metal apart sheared the heavy-duty internal bolts and split the steel tower seam from the inside out, leading to sudden, total structural failure.

"Ice-jacking is an insidious process because it works quietly from the inside out, completely hidden from visual inspections," Sparks noted. "Water found a pathway into the tower's internal sleeve, and as it froze, the expanding ice generated forces far beyond what the steel joint was designed to withstand. It effectively acted as a hydraulic jack, forcing the structural components apart."

### A Dark Echo: The 2006 Silver Mountain Incident

The Whistler accident sent shockwaves through the global ski industry, largely because it mirrored a strikingly similar, highly publicized incident just two years earlier in the United States. 

In January 2006, at Silver Mountain Resort in Kellogg, Idaho, a support tower on the resort's 3.1-mile gondola suffered a structural failure under remarkably similar circumstances. Rain and snowmelt had seeped into an unvented splice joint on a hollow steel tower. Subsequent sub-zero temperatures caused the trapped water to freeze, creating an ice-jack that ruptured the steel shell and compromised the tower’s structural integrity. 

While the Silver Mountain incident resulted in no serious injuries, it served as the industry’s first major warning sign regarding the dangers of trapped water in hollow lift infrastructure. The Whistler collapse proved that the vulnerability was not an isolated defect, but an industry-wide engineering hazard for lifts built with similar telescoping tower designs.

### Industry-Wide Aftermath

In the wake of the Excalibur collapse, safety regulators across North America mandated immediate inspections of thousands of hollow steel lift towers. Lift manufacturers, including Doppelmayr, issued imperative service bulletins requiring operators to drill drainage holes in tower bases and joints, install internal seals, and utilize ultrasound technology to scan for hidden moisture accumulation or internal bolt fractures.

Whistler Blackcomb subsequently retrofitted the Excalibur Gondola with enhanced drainage systems and structural reinforcements before reopening the lift. 

While the accident permanently altered lift maintenance and inspection protocols worldwide, it remains best remembered in Whistler for the harrowing afternoon 53 passengers spent suspended over the mountain—and the engineering anomaly that silently brought a massive steel tower to its knees.

On **December 16, 2008**, a major structural failure occurred on the **Excalibur Gondola** at the Whistler Blackcomb ski resort in British Columbia, Canada. It remains one of the most high-profile lift accidents in North American ski history. 

Here is a breakdown of what happened, why the tower failed, and how the trapped passengers were rescued.

---

### 1. What Happened?
At around 2:30 PM on a cold afternoon, **Tower 4** of the Excalibur Gondola suddenly sheared and collapsed near its upper section. 

* The collapse caused the heavy steel haul cable to drop rapidly, sending a massive shockwave down the line.
* Two gondola cabins plunged to the ground: one slammed into the roof of a nearby condo estate, while another dropped into a frozen creek bed below. 
* Dozens of other cabins were left dangling precariously in mid-air, swaying violently.
* A total of **53 passengers** were trapped inside suspended cabins scattered along the lower section of the mountain.
* Miraculously, **no one was killed**, though 12 people suffered injuries ranging from minor bruises to broken bones and spinal trauma.

---

### 2. Why Did the Tower Snap?
An extensive investigation by the BC Safety Authority revealed the cause to be a phenomenon known as **"ice jacking."**

* **Water Seepage:** Water had managed to seep into the hollow interior of the steel tower through small cracks or unsealed joints near the top of the structure.
* **Freeze-Thaw Cycles:** Over time, as temperatures fluctuated above and below freezing, the trapped water repeatedly froze and expanded. 
* **Structural Rupture:** The immense internal pressure generated by the expanding ice—which can exert thousands of pounds of pressure per square inch—gradually split the steel tube from the inside out. 
* **Catastrophic Failure:** On the day of the incident, the structural integrity of the tower had been weakened to the point where it could no longer support the weight and tension of the moving gondola line, causing the top section to snap off.

Prior to this incident, "ice jacking" in hollow lift towers was not widely recognized as a major risk in the ski industry. The discovery led to immediate safety overhauls, requiring resorts worldwide to drill drainage holes and inspect hollow steel towers for trapped water.

---

### 3. How Were the People Rescued?
With temperatures dropping below freezing and night approaching, Whistler Ski Patrol and local emergency services launched a massive, highly coordinated rope rescue operation.

* **Climbing to the Cabins:** Rescuers used specialized gear to scale the intact towers along the line. From there, patrollers used a "cable cyclist" (a rolling harness device) to traverse along the steel cable directly to the stranded cabins.
* **Gaining Access:** Rescuers shimmed open the top emergency hatches or forced open the side doors of the dangling gondola cars.
* **Lowering Passengers:** Rescuers secured each passenger into a harness or rescue seat, attached them to a heavy-duty rope system, and manually lowered them one by one down to the ground—in some places, dropping people up to 30 to 100 feet.
* **Ground Support:** Below, ground crews dressed in heavy winter gear greeted the passengers, provided warm blankets and hot drinks, and triaged anyone with injuries. 

Despite the extreme cold, high height, and tricky terrain, the rescue team successfully evacuated all **53 trapped passengers in just under three hours**. Their swift action prevented severe cases of hypothermia or panic.

Both remain in stable condition.
*   **Fatalities:** 0

"The terrain beneath Towers 3 and 4 is steep and heavily forested, which severely hampered our ability to position ground vehicles," said Sarah Jenkins, Regional SAR Incident Commander. "Rope rescue teams had to climb every affected tower in the dark, manually lower technicians onto the cabins, and lower passengers one by one. It was a painstaking, high-risk effort, but zero fatalities is a testament to the crew's training."

### Cause of the Rupture: Freeze-Thaw and Internal Corrosion

A preliminary report released Thursday morning by Technical Safety BC (TSBC), the province’s oversight body for passenger ropeways, identified the root cause as a failure of the tower’s hollow tubular steel column. 

Investigators found that melting snow and heavy rains earlier in the season had seeped into the interior of the sealed steel tower through a degraded weather seal near the top crossarm joint. Over time, the trapped water pooled at a internal structural baffle near the tower's midpoint. 

When an intense Arctic cold front swept through B.C. earlier this week, the trapped water froze. Because water expands by roughly nine percent when freezing, it exerted immense, localized internal hydraulic pressure against the structural steel walls. Combined with undetected internal corrosion that had thinned the steel from the inside out, the force exceeded the tower's structural yield strength, causing the metal to tear open along a vertical seam and buckle under the weight of the haul cable.

"This was not a failure of the cable or the mechanical grips holding the cabins," explained Senior TSBC Investigator Marcus Vance. "The cable held, which prevented a far worse catastrophe. This was an internal structural rupture caused by trapped liquid turning to ice—essentially, the steel pipe burst like an uninsulated home water pipe during a deep freeze."

### System-Wide Inspection Results

In the wake of the failure, TSBC immediately ordered the resort—and four other operators in B.C. utilizing similar hollow-steel tower designs—to suspend operations pending comprehensive non-destructive testing (NDT).

Engineers utilized ultrasonic thickness testing, thermal imaging, and endoscopes to inspect the remaining 18 towers on the affected line, as well as dozens of towers on neighboring lifts. 

The inspection results, published late Thursday, revealed concerning vulnerabilities:
*   **Water Ingress:** Three other towers on the same lift line were found to contain standing internal water.
*   **Micro-fracturing:** One adjacent tower exhibited early-stage surface cracking near a welded joint, attributed to stress amplification caused by localized ice pressure.
*   **Drainage Blockages:** Five towers across two different regional resorts were found to have obstructed internal drainage channels.

TSBC has stated that all towers containing moisture have been drained, flushed, and subjected to structural integrity re-certification. The affected gondola line will remain closed indefinitely until a replacement tower is installed and full safety clearances are issued.

### Expert Analysis: The Vital Role of Drainage Holes and Preventative Maintenance

The incident has sparked intense discussion among ropeway engineers regarding maintenance protocols for hollow steel structures used in extreme alpine environments.

Dr. Aris Thorne, a professor of structural engineering at the University of British Columbia and an expert in cold-weather mechanics, emphasized that while structural design is rigorous, reliance on "watertight seals" alone is a flawed strategy.

"In civil and mechanical engineering, we operate under a simple rule: assume water will always find a way in," Dr. Thorne said in an interview. "The ultimate line of defense against freeze-thaw damage isn't sealing the water out—it’s giving the water a clear, unhindered pathway to escape."

Dr. Thorne highlighted the critical importance of properly designed and maintained **weep holes** (drainage holes) at the base and internal levels of hollow steel columns.

"A simple two-inch drainage hole at the base of a structural baffle acts as a safety valve," Thorne explained. "If water enters at the top, it simply drains out the bottom before it can accumulate. However, in alpine conditions, these weep holes can become clogged by internal rust flakes, road salt crystals, or migrating protective grease. If a resort's maintenance checklist only looks at the *outside* of the tower, they miss the catastrophic process happening within."

Thorne advocated for three immediate preventative changes industry-wide:
1.  **Mandatory Internal Endoscopic Inspections:** Annual insertion of flexible cameras into tower drain ports to check for standing water and internal rust.
2.  **Heat-Traced or Enlarged Weep Holes:** Ensuring drainage ports are large enough to resist clogging and positioned to prevent ice caps from sealing them shut.
3.  **Internal Anti-Corrosion Coatings:** Applying wax- or oil-based rust inhibitors inside hollow columns during manufacturing and major overhauls.

### Response and Next Steps

The resort’s Chief Executive Officer issued an apology to guests and praised the emergency responders during a Thursday press briefing. 

"We are deeply sorry for the terrifying experience our guests endured on Tuesday," the CEO said. "While our maintenance protocols met all current regulatory standards, those standards clearly need to evolve. We are working fully with Technical Safety BC to implement every recommendation, including retrofitting all towers with upgraded drainage systems and advanced internal monitoring."

Technical Safety BC announced it will host an emergency summit next week with operators from across the province to standardize new internal inspection criteria for all hollow-structure ski lifts ahead of the peak winter holiday season.

**‘A Hydraulic Jack Made of Ice’: Trapped Water Ruptures Gondola Tower in Rare Structural Failure**

**SILVER PEAK, Colo.** — Before the first chairlifts were set to turn on Tuesday morning, a deafening crack echoed across the alpine bowl at Silver Peak Resort. Maintenance workers initially mistook the sound for avalanche mitigation artillery. 

Instead, they discovered a sight that forensic engineers are calling a "one-in-a-million" structural anomaly: Tower 6, a 65-foot steel support column for the resort’s primary summit gondola, had torn wide open from the inside out. 

The catastrophic rupture severed a vertical seam near a critical mid-tower splice, causing the top section of the steel column to buckle sideways. Emergency mechanical brakes on the haul rope engaged automatically, preventing the cable from sagging to the ground and avoiding what could have been a fatal accident had the lift been carrying passengers.

Resort officials immediately shut down the lift, and state tramway inspectors rushed to the scene. By Wednesday afternoon, independent metallurgists and structural engineers had pinpointed the silent, devastating cause of the failure: a phenomenon known as internal ice expansion, or "frost jacking," operating on a massive, industrial scale.

### A Pressure Vessel of Ice

Hollow, tubular steel towers are the backbone of modern ropeway infrastructure. To facilitate transportation and assembly, these multi-ton structures are constructed in sections and joined on-site using heavy, internal flange splices held together by high-strength bolts.

According to preliminary investigative reports, moisture had been secretly accumulating inside a hollow section of Tower 6 for years. Inspectors suspect a degraded rubber sealant gasket at a upper flange joint, combined with blocked condensation drainage weep holes at the tower’s base, allowed gallons of snowmelt and rainwater to collect undetected inside the sealed steel column.

When a sudden Arctic cold front slammed into the region Monday night, dropping temperatures from 38°F to -18°F in less than six hours, the trapped water rapidly froze.

As water converts to ice, its volume expands by roughly 9 percent. When contained within a rigid, unyielding space, that expansion generates exponential forces. 

"When water has nowhere to go as it freezes, it acts like a slow-motion hydraulic pump," said Dr. Marcus Vance, a forensic structural engineer with the National Institute for Infrastructure Safety, who was called in to examine the wreckage. "At -18 degrees, confined water can exert pressure exceeding 30,000 pounds per square inch. Across the surface area of that vertical splice, the ice was pushing outward with hundreds of tons of pressure—far exceeding the ultimate tensile strength of three-quarter-inch structural steel."

The steel wall finally yielded along a factory weld seam near the splice. The rupture sheared eight 1-inch grade-8 steel bolts instantly, causing the metal to tear open like a soda can subjected to an internal explosion.

### Industry-Wide Implications

While freeze-thaw cycles routinely damage pavement and concrete, the complete explosive destruction of a heavy steel lift tower due to internal water accumulation is virtually unprecedented in the North American ski industry. Most modern lift designs incorporate redundant drainage systems, internal anti-corrosion coatings, and strict moisture-monitoring protocols.

The Colorado Passenger Tramway Safety Board (CPTSB) issued an immediate directive ordering visual and ultrasonic moisture inspections for all hollow steel lift towers of similar design across the state. 

"Ski lifts are among the most heavily regulated and rigorously inspected conveyances in the world," said Elena Rostova, a spokesperson for the CPTSB. "This specific mechanism of failure is extraordinarily rare, but because it represents a catastrophic threat to structural integrity, every operator must ensure their tower drainage systems are clear before re-opening."

### Recovery and Investigation

Silver Peak Resort announced that the summit gondola will remain out of operation for the rest of the winter season. Removing and replacing Tower 6 will require building a temporary snow road to haul heavy machinery into the high-alpine zone, followed by the installation of a custom-fabricated steel section.

Resort management stressed that daily visual inspections had been performed, but acknowledged that internal water accumulation is impossible to detect visually from the outside until the steel begins to deform or fail.

"We are deeply relieved that this occurred during our pre-operational safety checks and that no guests or staff were injured," the resort said in a statement. "Safety is our absolute baseline, and we are working fully with state regulators and independent engineers to understand how this water bypassed our sealants and drainage protocols."

Forensic teams are currently using cranes to dismantle the damaged sections of Tower 6, which will be transported to a metallurgy laboratory in Denver for micro-structural analysis and ultrasonic mapping.

***

**Reported by:**  
*Julian Mercer, Senior Infrastructure & Mountain Operations Reporter*  
*With additional reporting by Clara Vance in Denver*  
*Field Photography by David Sterling*
